opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the more interesting open design problems right now. The way I think about it, there's a spectrum of options depending on how much signal you can actually get from the environment.

At the simplest end, you have outcome-based rewards. The agent calls a bunch of functions, eventually produces a final answer, and you just check whether that answer is right. If you have a verifiable task, like a math problem, a coding task with unit tests, or a database query where you know the expected result, this works surprisingly well. It's cheap, it's hard to game if your verifier is good, and it lets the model figure out its own strategy for which tools to use and when. The downside, of course, is sparsity. If the agent makes fifteen tool calls and gets the final answer wrong, you don't really know which of those calls was the problem.

So the next level is giving some intermediate or process-level reward on the function calls themselves. Some of that can be very mechanical: did the call parse correctly, did it match the schema, did it use valid argument types, did the API return an error or not. Those are almost free signals and they help a lot early in training, especially with smaller models that just struggle to format calls properly. But you have to be careful, because if you reward well-formed calls too heavily, the model learns to make lots of syntactically perfect, useless calls.

Then there's the more semantic layer: was this the right tool to call at this point, and were the arguments sensible? Here you can use a reference trajectory if you have one, comparing the agent's calls against a known-good sequence, though that tends to be brittle because there are often many valid paths. Or you can use an LLM as a judge to score each step, which is flexible but brings its own noise and potential for reward hacking.

I'd also mention efficiency-based shaping, penalizing redundant calls, excessive latency, or cost, because in production that matters a lot. An agent that gets the right answer with three calls is much better than one that needs thirty.

In practice, what I've seen work best is a combination: a strong outcome reward as the anchor, light format-level rewards to bootstrap, and maybe a small efficiency penalty, while being very skeptical of anything that's easy for the model to exploit. And honestly, a big part of the work isn't the reward function itself, it's building good environments and verifiers, because the reward is only as good as the signal you can actually check.

r001.rationale: It proposes using an LLM judge to score each step, including whether the chosen tool and its arguments were sensible.

r002.rationale: It identifies whether the API returned an error as a mechanical signal from executing a function call.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot at Bespoke, because once you're training agents with RL, the reward design basically becomes the whole game. And when the agent is calling tools or functions, there's a spectrum of options, and each one has tradeoffs.

The simplest thing you can do is what I'd call a structural or syntactic reward. Did the model produce a valid function call? Is the JSON well-formed, does the function name exist, are the argument types right? That's cheap, it's fully verifiable, and it's actually a surprisingly useful signal early in training because a lot of small models just can't even emit a correct call reliably. But it's also pretty shallow. A perfectly formatted call to the wrong tool with the wrong arguments gets full marks.

The next step up is matching against a reference. So you have a ground truth trajectory, maybe a human wrote it or a stronger model produced it, and you check whether the agent's call matches the expected function and arguments. This is where a lot of the function-calling benchmarks live. The problem is that there's often more than one correct way to do something. Maybe you search first and then read, or you read directly. If your reward only accepts one path, you end up penalizing perfectly good behavior and the policy learns to imitate the reference rather than actually solve the task. We've seen this really hurt generalization.

Then you get to what I think is the most interesting option, which is outcome-based reward. You don't care how the agent got there, you just execute the tools in a real or simulated environment and check whether the final state is correct. Did the database row get updated, did the test pass, did the right file end up in the right place? This is the closest thing to a verifiable reward in the agentic setting, the way math answers or unit tests are for code. And it lets the model discover its own strategies, which is where you see the emergent behaviors people get excited about.

But the catch with pure outcome reward is sparsity and credit assignment. If a task takes fifteen tool calls and the agent gets a single zero at the end, it's really hard to learn which of those fifteen steps was the mistake. So in practice you often want some shaping. You might give partial credit for intermediate milestones, or you reward progress toward the goal state, or you use a step-level judge. And that's where you have to be careful, because every bit of shaping is an opportunity for reward hacking. The model will find the shortest path to the reward, not to the task.

The last category is using an LLM as a judge over the trajectory. That's useful when the outcome isn't crisply verifiable, like a research task or a customer support interaction, where you want to evaluate whether the tool use was sensible and efficient. But you're now bootstrapping off another model's judgment, so you inherit its biases, and judges tend to be gameable in ways that are hard to anticipate.

So the way I'd summarize it: prefer verifiable outcomes wherever you can get them, build your environments so that outcomes are checkable, and only add shaping or judges when you have to. And whatever you do, look at the trajectories. Reading the rollouts is still the best way to find out that your reward is teaching the model something you didn't intend.

r001.rationale: Identifies an LLM judging a tool-use trajectory for whether the agent’s actions were sensible as a reward option.

r002.rationale: Identifies outcome-based reward from executing the tools and checking the resulting state, with examples such as whether a test passed or a database row was updated.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of ways to approach it. One is to reward the outcome: did the agent actually accomplish the task? You let it choose which functions to call, and you give it a reward based on the final result. That’s relatively simple, but the credit assignment becomes difficult if it takes a lot of calls to get there. Which calls actually helped?

The other option is to give more immediate feedback on the function use itself. Did it pick an appropriate function? Were the arguments correct? Did the call produce useful information? That gives you a denser reward signal, but you have to be careful that you’re not rewarding activity rather than progress. An agent could make perfectly valid calls that don’t help solve the problem.

So I’d think about combining those: use task success as the main objective, and then use intermediate feedback to help the agent learn, perhaps with a cost for unnecessary calls. The important thing is that calling a function is a means to accomplishing the task, rather than an objective on its own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a function was appropriate, but does not identify an LLM judging the agent’s text as the reward signal.

r002.rationale: It proposes feedback on whether a function call produced useful information, identifying the call’s result as a possible reward signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few ways to approach it. One is to reward the final outcome: did the agent actually solve the user’s problem? That gives you a clear objective, but if the agent makes a lot of function calls along the way, it’s hard to know which ones contributed to success.

Another option is to give more local feedback. Did it choose the right function? Did it provide the right arguments? Was the result useful for the next step? That gives you a denser signal, but you have to be careful that you’re not rewarding function calls just because they look reasonable.

So I’d think about combining those: use task success as the main signal, and then use intermediate feedback to help with credit assignment. You can also account for the cost of a call or its latency, because ideally the agent solves the problem efficiently, rather than making unnecessary calls.

r001.rationale: The response mentions judging whether a function choice and its arguments were right, but does not identify an LLM judging from the agent’s text whether its function use makes sense.

r002.rationale: It proposes local feedback on whether the function result was useful for the next step, identifying the returned result’s usefulness as a possible reward signal.
